chapter: Army service and the 816th Pioneer Infantry Band
title: Winning the bandmaster's job of the 816th Pioneer Infantry Band
summary: In an elimination contest White impressed the lieutenant and was made bandmaster; the band toured by train on Liberty drives to Camp Upton.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Me. Me. Nine fellas down the line held their hands up. Another rank over here. The sergeant was asking the same thing over there. About eleven from over there held their hands up. All right. All you men report to the YMC. So, into the YMC, well, about twenty-four of us. And when we assembled in the YMC, there was a lieutenant there, just out of the Chautauqua band. Canadian Kilties. You remember that band, the Canadian Kilties?

Oh, they were fine. We dated them down in Clovis, New Mexico one time. But that's either here or there. Anyhow, this fellow was already in his first lieutenant's uniform. And they had sent him to take charge of the 816th Pioneer Infantry Band. He held a rehearsal with we twenty-four fellas. And he says, I'll have another rehearsal tonight at nine o'clock. This is long, about six o'clock. That night at nine o'clock, we were all assembled in there again. He says, I'm going to have an elimination contest in here. He says, because I have gotten new orders. I'm going to be a line officer and there is promotion for me. And there is a chance for one of you men in this outfit to become the band leader of this regiment now being formed. He says, the 806th and the 805th Pioneer Infantry have already been formed. And they are now in regimented and in structures ready for sailing. Now this is my second day in camp. He says, one of you men in here are going to take charge of the 816th van temporarily. Because I'm going to recommend, so recommend it to the Colonel in charge here. And the Colonel of the 816th is going to be Colonel L.A. I. Chapman. Colonel Chapman he just called. I was learning his initials. And your Lieutenant Colonel is going to be Lieutenant Colonel Pottle. And Lieutenant Colonel Pottle will be over here in a few minutes because he wants this unit to do guard mount tomorrow. Okay, finally. So the first thing he put up is, Espanol Waltz. You don't want me to say that I guess. I remember that. Alright, so he put up that and he says, now I'm going to start conducting. And I'm not, I'm going to disregard all of your mistakes. But the man, when I am through conducting, if the man I find playing, as long as I'm conducting, and finishes up according to the measure or the strain where I am, that man will be considered the bandmaster here. So he went all the way down until he came to the, I think the C section. You know, Waltz is written there. C is the one. And where you have to, it's a Dalsignal sign there. And then you must go back up to the very first strain and then, we lay there at the end of that strain down to D. Well, he, when he, when he, when he observed his, that signal sound, or the kapo, and got back down that strain, he cut off. And you see, the thing of it is that I stress with my fellows always, you keep your eye glued here, but let the shadow of that baton be seen by you also. If you don't observe the shadow of this baton, you're not playing according to the direction. Yeah, I know you have to read the music down there, certainly, but the shadow of this baton will also be seen by you. Even if you read that music, you can keep one eye glued down here for your next measure, and you can still see the shadow of that baton. Of course, there's a little, little flair in there. I might as well tell you about it. I had played the waltz before. Wasn't anybody playing with me.

I said, Amos, Mordecai, White. Step out. Hey, fellas, here's your bandmaster. Now, I'll be a line officer, and good luck to you. You play a wonderful trumpet. I was playing then a JW York and son trumpet, and he had an EA Couturier trumpet. And that made me have a love for the Couturier horn, and I bought the 10,000th instrument. No, 1,000th some odd. 1076. My boy's got, my grandson has the trumpet out there now. 1076, designed by EA Couturier and Sons. La Porte, Indiana. After he came to America to demonstrate for the Holden Company. Well, then that began my tenure with the 816 Piney Infantry. In the next five days, we were on the train, making Liberty long drives in cities. The first city out of, out of, uh, Camp Funston was Kansas City, Missouri. And Kansas City, Missouri to St. Louis. St. Louis to Indianapolis. St. Louis to Columbus, Ohio. Columbus, Ohio to Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. And strangely, we jumped all the way back cross country, some roundabout way to Cleveland. And, uh, went up to, uh, Omaha, Nebraska, uh, to St. Paul. And, uh, doubled back in there, about three days riding, making Liberty long drives in various cities. And the band wasn't so well rehearsed, but they had a chance. We, they gave us a whole, uh, uh, boxcar. And we'd sit in this boxcar, and they'd serve us meals in there at these various points. And the Red Cross, and everybody else was giving us fine food on the route. And put birth in there for us. And then those travelers, the four days, the band became a very well-constructed unit. But when I got to, uh, uh, Camp Upton, Long Island, where I, they had recruited about seventeen more men out of Fort Riley. And they had sent them to me also. They came out with William Triggs. A fellow named William Triggs, who after they became my first sighted in the band. And then I got, I think I got about, uh, four fellas right out of Camp Upton. And the band's strength then was brought up to fully 47. 47. And we stayed in the water out there a day and a night, or maybe a little longer. I don't remember which one, I stayed seasick from the time I got on the boat until I got across almost.
